newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Fear of rebels grips Zaire port city of Matadi.
newsitem.headline: Fear of rebels grips Zaire port city of Matadi.

text.p: The military governor of Lower Zaire Province appealed on Thursday to local people to help the army defend Zaire's only seaport of Matadi against advancing rebels.
Admiral Liwanga Mada took over formally as emergency rule administrator on Wednesday amid rumours that Laurent Kabila's rebels had infiltrated Matadi, which borders Angola.

"We all have to save our region of Bas Zaire (Lower Zaire). I call for the support of all the people in the actions that the army needs to take to save Bas Zaire and the important city of Matadi," Liwanga said at a public ceremony.
Rebels on Wednesday said they captured three strategic towns in their advance on the capital Kinshasa, raising fears in the few major cities still in government hands.

Two days before the military governor arrived, panic swept through the town as soldiers evacuated their families from barracks following a false news report by a regional radio station that rebels had entered Matadi.
An embarrassed army commander went on local radio to say that troops had only been going through evacuation drills.
Security is tight in the city, which is full of men of the SNIP military intelligence.

Apart from its importance as the only seaport, Matadi is also close to Zaire's Inga hydro-electric dam, some 60 km (35 miles) to the east, the main source of power for Zaire and an important supplier to Congo and Zambia. Zaire's only oil refinery is at Muanda to the west.
The army has set up check points on both ends of the Japanese-built suspension bridge across the mighty Zaire river which disects Matadi before emptying into the Atlantic at Boma.
Many townspeople reported sighting strangers in taxis speaking English or Swahili, the common languages among Kabila's rebel army in which ethnic Tutsis are the spearhead.
"I saw three in a taxi last night speaking English," a resident said. "When the driver opened a door and the interior light came on I saw their faces. They were not Zairean."

The Angolan border is only about five km (three miles) outside Matadi and its government is said by regional analysts to back Kabila, who wants to topple Mobutu who in turn backed Angola's UNITA rebels for years.
Angola's national radio said the government tightened border controls with Zaire this week after an increase in people crossing into its diamond-rich Lunda Norte province.
Quoting the ministry of the interior, the radio reported on Wednesday that Angolan troops had detained 24 people, some of them armed, crossing the border illegally from Zaire.

Many Matadi residents said they were waiting for Kabila to come and take over the town but that they feared soldiers would go on a looting spree before then. In other towns taken by rebels, soldiers looted homes and businesses before fleeing.
The governor acknowledged this fear but tried to assure local people that Matadi would be different. He also accused civilians of looting in other towns to discredit the army.

"Looting is on everyone's mind. I don't think today the military have in their head the thought of looting, but some civilian authorities want to instill this in the head of the military," he said in his speech.
Despite the assurance, many traders are taking precautions. While most shops are open, storeowners have generally locked away most merchandise in secure warehouses.
Industry sources said some shipping companies were already reluctant to use Matadi port and some were now rerouting imports through Pointe-Noire in neighbouring Congo.
